# Before you start

Work in this file. Write your answers where each question asks for them, render it, and hand in both files at the end of class:

+ this `.qmd` file, with your own name in the `author` field at the top
+ the `.html` file you get from rendering it

Leave `embed-resources: true` alone, so your `.html` opens on my machine without any extra files. Render one last time before you submit, so I know the document runs from top to bottom.

Three questions. Each one has R parts, from lecture note 01, and one Quarto part about controlling what a code chunk shows. The Quarto parts name the chunk option to use, so use that one. Writing an answer as plain text where a chunk was asked for does not count, even when the R is right.

# Q1: element types and what `c()` does to them

(a) In a code chunk, create a vector called `nums` holding the numbers 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42, and print `class(nums)`. Show the code and the output.

(b) In a second chunk, create `mixed <- c(1, 2, "three")`, then print `mixed` and `class(mixed)`.

(c) In two or three sentences of plain text, say what happened to the numbers 1 and 2 in `mixed`, why R did that, and what you would get from `mixed[1] + 1`.

(d) **Quarto part.** Write a third chunk that runs `sum(nums)` with the code hidden, so a reader of your `.html` sees the result and no code. Use the chunk option `#| echo: false`. Hide the code, do not delete it.

# Q2: getting parts out of a `data.frame`

(a) In a code chunk, build this `data.frame`, call it `plots`, and print `str(plots)`:

+ `plot_id`: the character values "a", "b", "c", "d"
+ `yield`: the numbers 180, 205, 172, 198
+ `irrigated`: the logical values `TRUE`, `TRUE`, `FALSE`, `TRUE`

(b) In one chunk, pull out the `yield` column two ways, once with `$` and once with `[[ ]]`, then pull out the third row of the whole `data.frame`.

(c) A `data.frame` is a special kind of list. In one or two sentences of plain text, say what that means for its columns: what has to be true of the columns of a `data.frame` that need not be true of the elements of an ordinary list?

(d) **Quarto part.** Write this sentence in your document, with both blanks filled in by inline R code rather than typed by hand:

````
The `plots` data has `r nrow(plots)` rows and a mean yield of `r mean(plots$yield)` bushels.
````

Typing either number yourself gets no credit for this part. The point is that the sentence updates itself when the data changes.

# Q3: functions, arguments, and packages

(a) Run `?seq` in your console to see what arguments `seq()` takes. You do not have to show that in your document. Then, in a code chunk, use `seq()` with **named** arguments to create the sequence 0, 5, 10, ..., 100, assign it to `steps`, and print `length(steps)`.

(b) In one chunk, create `steps_na <- c(steps, NA)` and run `mean(steps_na)`. Then run `mean()` on the same vector again so that it returns a number. In one or two sentences of plain text, name the argument you added and say what it tells `mean()` to do.

(c) Run this line in your console:

````
mean(steps, na.rm)
````

In one or two sentences of plain text, quote the error message and say what R was complaining about.

(d) **Quarto part.** Two chunks. First, a chunk holding `install.packages("dplyr")` that is shown but never run, using `#| eval: false`. That is how you show a reader a command to run once themselves without running it on every render. Second, a chunk that runs `library(dplyr)` and then `glimpse(plots)`, with `#| message: false` and `#| warning: false` so the package startup messages stay out of your report. Install `dplyr` from your console first if you have not already.
